newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Europe cash cocoa trade ebbs, flows on stg moves.
newsitem.headline: Europe cash cocoa trade ebbs, flows on stg moves.

text.p: Cash cocoa buying picked up in Europe earlier this week but the pound's bounce against continental Europe currencies soon snuffed out the rekindled demand.
"We saw a little buying earlier in the week when sterling dropped against the mark and guilder but that dried up when the currency firmed and the market moved higher," one trader said.
Cocoa futures have risen by around 15 stg since last week, with benchmark July futures trading near 1,030 stg a tonne.
Traders said the Ivory Coast was in the market offering new crop beans and some also said Ghana was active, albeit to a lesser extend.
"Ivory Coast has been constantly in the market, but I doubt they will have done much business," one said.

Differentials have held steady, with Ivorian nearby cocoa offered at around 25 stg under the terminal, with similar levels seen for positions through to the end-year. Ghana was quoted at near 10 stg under but differentials improved further out, with positions next year quoted at levels above the terminal.

In Germany, traders said the public holidays had allowed many plants to undergo maintenance in May and this had reduced the need for spot purchases, but this was interpreted as a further indication that chocolate sales remained weak.

Despite the terminal's move higher later this week, some traders pointed to bearish factors earlier on, which had kept industry buying limited. High stocks in Europe have given the impression to many that there is abundant nearby material.
"From a fundamental viewpoint, the market looked as though it was going lower," a trader said.

In its latest report, warehousing firm SGS said stocks in Europe were running at over 900,000 tonnes with some 600,000 in Amsterdam alone. The total was somewhat lower then the previous month but given that Ivorian shipments had dwindled in the past few weeks, this was to be expected, traders said.
In addition to stocks, they said the latest weather reports from the Ivory Coast indicated that the new crop was progressing well, and would be of a good size.
"The main problem is an unwillingness on the part of industry to follow this market. They are still buying hand-to-mouth," one commented.

Against a bearish backdrop, physical traders said the futures market rose paradoxically, a move attributed to speculative buying linked to the large position believed to be held by U.S. trading house Phibro.
"Probably half of these European stocks are in one strong hand and that's a dominant market factor," one trader said.
